clinicalPearls: A benign but locally aggressive Schneiderian papilloma that typically arises from the lateral nasal wall and paranasal sinuses
Usually presents with unilateral nasal obstruction, discharge or epistaxis, which distinguishes it from bilateral inflammatory polyps
Any unilateral sinonasal mass or polyp warrants biopsy and imaging because of the risk of neoplasia
Named for its histology, in which the surface epithelium grows inward (inverts) into the underlying stroma
It carries a recognised risk of harbouring or progressing to squamous cell carcinoma, so occult malignancy must be excluded
CT helps define bony involvement and may show focal hyperostosis pointing to the tumour origin, while MRI can reveal a convoluted 'cerebriform' pattern and separate tumour from retained secretions
It has a marked tendency to recur, particularly after incomplete removal, so wide excision of the attachment with drilling of the underlying bone is advocated
Endoscopic resection has become the standard approach for most tumours, with long-term surveillance for recurrence
reference.pathophysiology: Inverted papilloma originates from the Schneiderian (ectodermally derived respiratory) mucosa lining the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. The hallmark is proliferation of the epithelium in an endophytic pattern, inverting into the stroma while maintaining an intact basement membrane. Although benign, it erodes and remodels adjacent bone and can extend widely through the sinuses, and it has a well-recognised association with squamous cell carcinoma arising synchronously or over time. Human papillomavirus has been implicated in some tumours, and the site of mucosal attachment is important because residual disease there drives recurrence.
additionalDifferentials: Other Schneiderian papillomas (exophytic or oncocytic types)
Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in young males
additionalInvestigations: Nasal endoscopy with biopsy of the lesion
CT of the paranasal sinuses to assess bony involvement and identify focal hyperostosis at the origin
MRI to define soft-tissue extent, detect the cerebriform pattern and distinguish tumour from retained secretions
Histopathological examination to confirm the inverted pattern and exclude coexisting malignancy
Imaging surveillance after resection to detect recurrence
redFlags: Features suggesting malignant transformation such as rapid growth, pain, or facial numbness
Orbital symptoms including proptosis, diplopia or visual disturbance
Intracranial extension or skull-base erosion on imaging
Recurrent unilateral epistaxis or a friable, bleeding mass
reference.prognosis: With complete excision including the site of attachment, most benign inverted papillomas are controlled, though recurrence is not uncommon and mandates long-term surveillance. When associated squamous cell carcinoma is present, prognosis depends on the stage and grade of that malignancy.
pitfalls: Assuming a unilateral nasal polyp is inflammatory and not obtaining histology
Incomplete removal of the mucosal attachment and underlying bone, leading to recurrence
Overlooking a focus of squamous cell carcinoma within the specimen
Mistaking retained sinus secretions for tumour on imaging without MRI correlation

management: Complete surgical excision, usually endoscopic, encompassing the mucosal attachment site with drilling of the underlying bone to minimise recurrence
Histopathological examination of the whole specimen to exclude synchronous squamous cell carcinoma
Escalation to oncological management appropriate to stage, including wider resection and adjuvant radiotherapy, where malignant transformation is present
Long-term endoscopic and imaging surveillance to detect recurrence at the attachment site
Coordinated otolaryngology and head-and-neck care, with skull-base team input when the tumour extends intracranially or into the orbit
